## Why a chapter on something that is not a measure

GRBAS and the CAPE-V are auditory-perceptual rating instruments. A listener
hears a voice and scores it on named dimensions. Neither is computed from a
signal, and neither is an acoustic measure.

They are here because every composite index in Part IV was fitted against them,
and because every diagnostic threshold in this reference was obtained by asking
how well an acoustic value separates two groups that a perceptual instrument
defined. A cutoff is a statement about a perceptual standard as much as about a
measure. Change the instrument, change the dimension, or move the point on the
scale at which a voice counts as affected, and the cutoff moves without
anything about the acoustics changing.

That is the argument of [Pipeline Dependence and Reference
Values](foundations-pipeline.qmd), one layer up. A measured value belongs to
the pipeline that produced it; a *cutoff* belongs to the pipeline and to the
perceptual standard that defined its groups.

The ASHA expert panel treats auditory-perceptual assessment with the CAPE-V as
a separate, non-instrumental part of a voice evaluation, accompanying acoustic,
laryngeal-imaging and aerodynamic assessment rather than being replaced by them
[@patel2018protocol]. Nothing in this reference argues otherwise. An acoustic
index approximates a perceptual judgement; it does not supersede it.

## GRBAS

The scale was proposed by the Committee for Phonatory Function Tests of the
Japan Society of Logopedics and Phoniatrics, for evaluating hoarseness. It
consists of five scales [@hirano1981clinical].

| Scale | What it represents | Stated acoustic correlate |
|---|---|---|
| G, grade | The degree of hoarseness or voice abnormality; it corresponds to the factor of evaluative nature obtained by the semantic differential technique | — |
| R, rough | The psycho-acoustic impression of irregularity of vocal fold vibrations | Irregular fluctuations in the fundamental frequency and/or the amplitude of the glottal source sound |
| B, breathy | The psycho-acoustic impression of the extent of air leakage through the glottis | Related to turbulence |
| A, asthenic | Weakness or lack of power in the voice | A weak intensity of the glottal source sound and/or a lack of higher harmonics |
| S, strained | The psycho-acoustic impression of a hyperfunctional state of phonation | An abnormally high fundamental frequency, noise in the high frequency range, and/or richness in high frequency harmonics |

: The five GRBAS scales and the acoustic correlates stated for them in the original description [@hirano1981clinical]. {#tbl-grbas}

**Each scale is graded on four points: 0 non-hoarse or normal, 1 slight, 2
moderate, 3 extreme** [@hirano1981clinical]. A result is written as the five
scores together, so a GRBAS rating is a profile rather than a number.

Two cautions come from the proposing committee itself. The evaluation is
subjective, so the examiner must possess a trained ear, and a standard tape of
typical voice samples was made for training. And the committee states that
psycho-acoustic evaluation with the GRBAS scale is not an absolute method and
needs to be improved upon [@hirano1981clinical]. Both remarks are from 1981 and
neither has been overtaken.

## CAPE-V

The CAPE-V was developed under ASHA Special Interest Division 3, first released
in 2002 and revised in 2009 [@patel2018protocol]. It is scored on a visual
analog scale, and its dimensions include overall severity, roughness,
breathiness, strain, pitch and loudness [@walden2022pvqd]. Its sentences,
recorded for the auditory-perceptual assessment of voice quality, can also
serve as the connected-speech sample for cepstral analysis [@patel2018protocol].

::: {.callout-warning}
**This reference does not yet describe the CAPE-V from its own documentation.**
The 2009 revision (Kempster and colleagues, as cited by @patel2018protocol) is
the instrument's source of record for its tasks, its visual anchors and its
scoring, and it is not yet in this project's source library. Until it is, this
chapter states only what other sources report about the instrument. That is a
declared absence of a source, in the same spirit as a declared absence of a
reference value: see [Pipeline Dependence](foundations-pipeline.qmd).
:::

## Averaging, and the thresholds it creates

Both instruments are applied by individual listeners. Every validation study in
this reference uses a **mean across raters** as its reference value.

That has a consequence worth stating plainly. Averaging turns GRBAS from a
four-point ordinal scale into a continuum, which is why thresholds such as a
mean grade of 0.5 exist at all. No single rater can return 0.5 on a scale whose
points are 0, 1, 2 and 3. The threshold is a property of the panel, not of a
judgement any listener made.

## The reference standards behind this reference's cutoffs

@tbl-anchor-standards is the set of perceptual standards that the cutoff
studies cited in Part III and Part IV actually used. The column that matters is
the third one.

| Study and language | Instrument | A voice counted as affected when | Raters and reliability |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dutch, AVQI external validation | GRBAS grade, mean | $G_\text{mean} \geq 0.5$ | — |
| Brazilian Portuguese, AVQI and ABI | GRBAS grade and breathiness, means | G < 0.5 and B < 0.5 taken as unaffected | five judges; Fleiss $\kappa$ 0.370 for G, 0.353 for B |
| Finnish, ABI | GRBAS breathiness, mean | a nonbreathy voice was one rated B 0–0.49 | eight listeners; Fleiss $\kappa$ 0.435 |
| Malayalam and Kannada, ABI | GRBAS breathiness | "B" of GRBAS as the reference standard | — |
| US English, AVQI and ABI | GRBAS grade, mean | $G_\text{mean} \geq 0.5$, stated for both indices | — |
| American English, PVQD, AVQI and CPPS | CAPE-V overall severity, 100-point scale | severity $\geq$ 10 | nineteen raters, three per file |
| American English, PVQD, AVQI | GRBAS grade, mean | grade $\geq$ 0.5 | as above |
| American English, PVQD, ABI | CAPE-V breathiness, 100-point scale | breathiness $\geq$ 10 | as above |
| Six ABI validations, pooled | GRBAS, means | per study | three to five judges per study; Fleiss $\kappa$ 0.353 to 0.492 |

: Perceptual reference standards used by the validation studies behind this reference's thresholds. Dutch: @barsties2016avqi; Brazilian Portuguese: @englert2020material and @englert2019abstract; Finnish: @kankare2023abi; Malayalam and Kannada: @jayakumar2024abi; US English: @castillo2023avqi; American English PVQD: @lucero2026phonalab with @walden2022pvqd; pooled: @barsties2021abi. {#tbl-anchor-standards}

Two of those choices carry a stated rationale. On the 100-point scale, 10 was
selected as a clinically meaningful boundary between normal variation and
minimal perceptible deviance; on the averaged ordinal scale, 0.5 is the
midpoint between normal and minimal severity [@lucero2026phonalab].

The ABI meta-analysis records a reliability floor for this literature: an
inter-rater Fleiss $\kappa$ of 0.41 is the recommended minimum, and the one
included study that fell below it is the one whose correlation between ABI and
perceived breathiness was lowest [@barsties2021abi].

## The PVQD, in detail

The Perceptual Voice Qualities Database is the sample behind this reference's
American English rows, so its rating procedure deserves its own section.

Its 296 recordings were rated by nineteen experienced voice clinicians using
voice qualities from the CAPE-V, **without visual anchors**, and the GRBAS
scale [@walden2022pvqd]. Raters had to be voice professionals with at least two
years of experience, familiar with both scales and using at least one of them
monthly; twenty-five were recruited and nineteen completed [@walden2022pvqd].

| Scale | Inter-rater ICC | Intra-rater ICC |
|---|---|---|
| 100-point visual analog | 0.86 | 0.913 |
| GRBAS | 0.859 | 0.889 |

: Reliability of the PVQD ratings for the database as a whole, with averages used as the ratings [@walden2022pvqd]. By dimension, inter-rater ICC was 0.918 for overall severity and 0.827 for breathiness on the visual analog scale, and 0.911 for grade and 0.844 for breathiness on GRBAS. {#tbl-pvqd-reliability}

Three cautions apply to those figures, and all three come from the database
paper itself [@walden2022pvqd].

**They are reliability for a mean of several raters.** The ICCs assume final
ratings based on three raters for inter-rater reliability and two repeated
ratings for intra-rater reliability, and were corrected upward with the
Spearman-Brown formula to account for the higher number of ratings per target.
A single clinician rating a voice alone is not at 0.918.

**They are consistency, not agreement.** Because different raters rated
different subsets of the database, reliability can only be assessed as
consistency between or within raters, under Shrout and Fleiss's ICC(1, *m*)
model. The design cannot assess agreement in the levels of the ratings. The
same non-overlapping assignment is why the validation study built on this
database could not model individual rater effects and used the published means
instead [@lucero2026phonalab].

**The severity scale is CAPE-V-like, not the CAPE-V.** Its dimensions were
borrowed from the CAPE-V and scored on a 100-point visual analog scale without
the instrument's visual anchors. A threshold written as "CAPE-V overall
severity $\geq$ 10" on this database is a threshold on that scale.

One further point concerns what "vocally healthy" means here. The database
paper reports 296 speakers, of whom 89 had no voice complaint, 187 reported a
complaint or had a confirmed diagnosis of dysphonia, and 20 have no data
recorded for voice complaint or diagnosis [@walden2022pvqd]. The validation
study using it reports 290 usable speakers as 181 with voice disorders and 109
vocally healthy [@lucero2026phonalab]. The arithmetic reconciles only if the 20
speakers with no recorded voice status are counted among the 109 controls, and
all six exclusions came from the disordered group. On that reading, roughly one
in five of the controls behind this reference's American English specificity
figures has no documented voice status. The inference is from the counts in the
two papers, and it should be confirmed against the database labels before it is
relied on.

## How to read a threshold

- **A threshold inherits its reference standard.** A cutoff validated against
  mean GRBAS grade answers the question "would a panel of listeners have called
  this voice hoarse?". A cutoff validated against CAPE-V breathiness answers a
  different question about a different dimension. A measure may separate one
  well and the other poorly, which is the point of a dimension-targeted index:
  see [ABI](abi.qmd) and [GNE](gne.qmd).
- **Two reference standards on one sample are not two validations.** Where a
  study reports the same cutoff against both CAPE-V severity and GRBAS grade,
  that is one sample analysed twice. See [AVQI](avqi.qmd).
- **A dichotomised perceptual rating is a summary, not a diagnosis.** The
  instruments grade a voice. They do not identify a lesion or a mechanism
  [@patel2018protocol].
- **Report the instrument, the dimension and the threshold** whenever a cutoff
  is quoted, exactly as the pipeline is reported for the measure itself.

## Where the sources disagree

**Where "normal" ends on an averaged GRBAS grade.** The database paper's own
figure categories place the normal band at 0 to 0.5, mild at 0.6 to 1.5,
moderate at 1.6 to 2.5 and severe at 2.6 to 3.0 [@walden2022pvqd]. The
validation literature treats a mean grade of 0.5 or above as affected
[@barsties2016avqi]. A voice with a mean grade of exactly 0.5 is therefore
normal under the first convention and dysphonic under the second. No value in
this reference is moved on account of it. The point matters because the
boundary sits where the ratings are densest: the PVQD's severity distribution
is skewed toward the normal, mild and moderate levels, and perception of
mild-to-moderate severities is harder than of normal and severe ones
[@walden2022pvqd].

**Whether rating scales are reliable enough to serve as a reference standard at
all.** The database paper establishes good inter- and intra-rater reliability
for the PVQD overall and concludes that its ratings may be used with relative
confidence for research [@walden2022pvqd]. A standard textbook treatment
reaches a much darker verdict about dimensional rating protocols as measurement
tools: across studies, scales and statistics, average interrater reliability
has ranged from extremely low ($r^2 = .04$) to extremely high; listeners almost
never agree in their ratings of a single voice; the likelihood that two raters
agree on moderately pathological voices on seven-point scales averaged 0.21
where chance is 0.14; and more than 60%, and as much as 78%, of the variance in
voice quality ratings was attributable to factors other than differences among
voices in the quality being rated [@kreiman2011foundations].

Both can hold at once, and the difference is in what is being measured. The
ICCs are for a mean of three trained raters on one database. The textbook
figures are for individual listeners judging individual voices across the
literature. The practical consequence is the same either way, and it is why
this chapter exists: the perceptual threshold is the softest element in any
acoustic cutoff, and it should be reported rather than assumed.
